title: II. He Gets Rid Of His Eldest Son
section: Book I — The History Of A Family
paragraphs: You can easily imagine what sort of father a man like that could be and how he'd raise his children. His behavior as a father was exactly what you'd expect. He completely abandoned the child of his marriage with Adelaïda Ivanovna, not out of malice, nor because of his marital grievances, but simply because he forgot him. While he was wearing everyone out with his tears and complaints, and turning his house into a sinkhole of debauchery, a faithful family servant, Grigory, took the three-year-old Mitya into his care. If he hadn't looked after him, there wouldn't have been anyone even to change the baby's little shirt.

It also happened that the child's relatives on his mother's side forgot him at first, too. His grandfather was no longer living, his widow—Mitya's grandmother—had moved to Moscow and was seriously ill, and his daughters were married, so Mitya remained for nearly a whole year in old Grigory's care, living with him in the servants' cottage. But even if his father had remembered him (he couldn't have been entirely unaware of his existence), he would have sent him back to the cottage, since the child would only have gotten in the way of his debaucheries. Then a cousin of Mitya's mother, Pyotr Alexandrovitch Miüsov, happened to return from Paris. He lived abroad for many years afterwards, but at the time was still a young man, distinguished among the Miüsovs as a man of enlightened ideas and European culture, who had been in the capitals and abroad. Toward the end of his life he became a Liberal of the kind common in the forties and fifties. Over the course of his career he had come into contact with many of the most Liberal men of his time, both in Russia and abroad. He had known Proudhon and Bakunin personally, and in his later years was very fond of describing the three days of the Paris Revolution of February 1848, hinting that he himself had almost taken part in the fighting on the barricades. This was one of the fondest memories of his youth. He had an independent property of about a thousand souls, to count in the old style. His splendid estate lay on the outskirts of our little town and bordered on the lands of our famous monastery, with which Pyotr Alexandrovitch started an endless lawsuit, almost as soon as he came into the estate, about fishing rights in the river or timber rights in the forest, I don't know exactly which. He considered it his duty as a citizen and a man of culture to open an attack on the "clericals." Hearing all about Adelaïda Ivanovna, whom of course he remembered and in whom he had at one time been interested, and learning of Mitya's existence, he stepped in, despite all his youthful indignation and contempt for Fyodor Pavlovitch. He made Fyodor Pavlovitch's acquaintance for the first time and told him straight out that he wanted to take charge of the child's upbringing. He used to tell, long afterwards, as a characteristic touch, that when he began to speak of Mitya, Fyodor Pavlovitch looked for some time as though he didn't understand what child he was talking about, and even seemed surprised to hear that he had a little son in the house. The story may have been exaggerated, but it must have been something close to the truth.

Fyodor Pavlovitch loved theatrics all his life—suddenly playing some unexpected part, sometimes without any motive whatsoever, and even to his own direct disadvantage, as in the present case. This habit, however, is characteristic of a great many people, some of them very clever ones, unlike Fyodor Pavlovitch. Pyotr Alexandrovitch pushed the business through vigorously and was appointed, along with Fyodor Pavlovitch, joint guardian of the child, who had a small property—a house and land—left to him by his mother. Mitya did indeed pass into this cousin's keeping, but since the cousin had no family of his own and, after securing the revenues of his estates, was in a hurry to return to Paris, he left the boy with one of his cousins, a lady living in Moscow. It so happened that, having settled permanently in Paris, he too forgot the child, especially when the February Revolution broke out, leaving an impression on his mind that he remembered all the rest of his life. The Moscow lady died, and Mitya passed into the care of one of her married daughters. I believe he changed homes a fourth time later on. I won't expand on that now, because I'll have much to tell later about Fyodor Pavlovitch's firstborn, and for now I must stick to the essential facts about him, without which I couldn't begin my story.

To start with, this Mitya—or rather, Dmitri Fyodorovitch—was the only one of Fyodor Pavlovitch's three sons who grew up believing that he had property and would be independent when he came of age. He spent an irregular boyhood and youth. He didn't finish his studies at the gymnasium, got into a military school, then went to the Caucasus, was promoted, fought a duel, was demoted to the ranks, earned promotion again, led a wild life, and spent a good deal of money. He didn't begin to receive any income from Fyodor Pavlovitch until he came of age, and until then he piled up debts. He saw and knew his father, Fyodor Pavlovitch, for the first time when he came of age and traveled to our neighborhood specifically to settle the matter of his property with him. He seems not to have liked his father. He didn't stay long and hurried to get away, having only managed to obtain a sum of money and entering into an agreement for future payments from the estate, whose revenues and value he was unable (a fact worth noting), on that occasion, to get any account of from his father. Fyodor Pavlovitch remarked for the first time then (this too should be noted) that Mitya had a vague and inflated idea of his property. Fyodor Pavlovitch was very well satisfied with this, since it fit in perfectly with his own plans. He gathered only that the young man was frivolous, unruly, of violent passions, impatient, and dissolute, and that if he could just get some ready cash he would be content—for a short time, of course. So Fyodor Pavlovitch began to take advantage of this, sending him small handouts from time to time, installments. In the end, when four years later Mitya, losing patience, came a second time to our little town to settle things with his father once and for all, it turned out, to his amazement, that he had nothing—that it was even hard to get an account, that he had already received the full value of his property in sums of money from Fyodor Pavlovitch, and was perhaps even in debt to him; that by various agreements he had, of his own accord, entered into at various previous times, he had no right to expect anything more, and so on, and so on. The young man was stunned, suspected deceit and cheating, and was almost beside himself. And indeed this circumstance led to the catastrophe whose account forms the subject of my first introductory story—or rather, the external side of it. But before I move on to that story, I must say a little about Fyodor Pavlovitch's other two sons, and where they came from.
